one_liner: Paul Hsieh's SuperFastHash as a tiny npm module in JS and AssemblyScript Wasm; Wasm about 1.2x the JS port on Node.
what_it_does: Computes the 32-bit SuperFastHash (non-cryptographic) of a byte array, returning a signed 32-bit integer. require('superfasthash') gives the plain JavaScript version; require('superfasthash/wasm') gives the same hash(message) function backed by a 355-byte AssemblyScript Wasm module embedded in dist/wasm/superfasthash.js, which only works after the promise from initialize() resolves. The two builds are interchangeable at the call site, and the repo's tests check that they agree on 1,000 random messages.
how_it_is_fast: The Wasm build copies the message into linear memory at offset 0 (Uint8ClampedArray.set) and runs the hash loop as native i32 arithmetic with one 4-byte i32.load per round. The JS port instead reads bytes one at a time and coerces every intermediate with >>> 0. The algorithm is SuperFastHash (16-bit add/shift/xor rounds plus a final avalanche); there is no SIMD and no batching. Each call still pays a JS-to-Wasm transition and a memcpy, so the gain is small.
when_to_use: You need SuperFastHash values inside a JS/Node codebase (for example to bucket or dedupe byte strings) and want a dependency-free, ISC-licensed file you can vendor.
Long-running processes that hash many small-to-medium messages (hundreds of bytes), where V8 has tiered up and the Wasm path's roughly 1.1-1.5x edge over the JS port is worth an async init.
Environments without Wasm: the pure-JS hash() has the same API and output, so you can fall back to it.
when_not_to_use: When you need hashes that match C/C++ SuperFastHash (Hsieh's hash.c, Chromium's base/third_party copy): both ports read the tail bytes as unsigned where the reference casts them to signed char, so about a quarter of random binary inputs hash differently (see gotchas).

Messages larger than 64 KiB on the Wasm path with default options: the module exports a 0-page memory that initialize() grows by one page, so wasmMemory.set() throws a RangeError unless you call initialize({ memory: N }) with enough 64 KiB pages.
Anything adversarial or security-relevant: it is a weak 32-bit non-cryptographic hash, and the repo's own tests assert collisions ('s11000' vs 's10018', 's99999' vs 's98981').

If you want a maintained, faster Wasm hash: the project has 9 commits, the last on 2019-04-06, it is not published on npm (the registry returns 404 for 'superfasthash'; install is from GitHub), and the build depends on AssemblyScript's 2019 master branch.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (prebuilt dist/wasm/superfasthash.js embeds the Wasm bytes); rebuilding needs assemblyscript from GitHub master and uglify-js
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js >= 10.10.0 (package.json engines); WebAssembly support for the wasm entry point
integration.platforms: any JS engine with WebAssembly (Node, browsers); pure-JS fallback everywhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the Wasm build keeps one module-level memory buffer and writes each message to offset 0, so each instance is single-threaded by construction (per JS realm)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same hash(message) signature and output as the module's JS version, but the Wasm entry point needs an awaited initialize() first, and the input must be a typed array or array of byte values

gotchas: Output differs from Paul Hsieh's reference C code: the reference (and Chromium's copy) does `hash += (signed char)*data` for a 1-byte tail and `(signed char)data[2] << 18` for a 3-byte tail, while both the JS and the AssemblyScript ports use the unsigned byte. A Python re-implementation of both, checked against the repo's ASCII test vectors, found 24.5% of 20,000 random 1-1000 byte messages hash differently from the reference (single byte 0xFF: reference 0, port -1444309403). The repo's fixed vectors are all ASCII, so its tests cannot catch this; JS and Wasm agree with each other.

The Wasm memory is 64 KiB by default (exported memory starts at 0 pages, initialize() grows it by options.memory = 1), so a longer message throws RangeError from wasmMemory.set; pass initialize({ memory: pages }) up front.

Benchmark harness (benchmarks/benchmark.js): one console.time pass per implementation over the same 1,000,000 crypto.randomBytes messages (about 500 MB in total), with no warm-up or repetition and the JS pass first. Issue #1 shows how much this moves the ratio: an earlier build measured JS 619 ms vs Wasm 683 ms (Wasm slower), the author later measured 440 vs 387 ms, the README screenshot shows 447.7 vs 369.1 ms (1.21x), and MaxGraey's PR #2 run shows 510.6 vs 338.3 ms (1.51x, derived from page data). At 1-1,000 hashes the author's table is dominated by JS warm-up (0.366 ms vs 0.080 ms for one hash).

The 'native' MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256/RIPEMD-160 rows call crypto.Hash(algo).update(msg).digest() per message, so they measure Node's per-object binding overhead plus a cryptographic hash, not a like-for-like baseline; the 10-12x gap over SuperFastHash says little about either.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you specifically need SuperFastHash in JS and accept its unsigned-tail deviation; for a general fast non-cryptographic hash in JS, the catalogued hash-wasm (XXHash64 about 16 GB/s vs xxhashjs) and xxhash-wasm entries are faster, maintained and published on npm. Among small AssemblyScript ports in this category it is similar in scale to xoroshiro128starstar (about 1.10x over Math.random): a modest, single-run gain.
verified_claims_summary: One first-party run on an unnamed Mac (Node and V8 versions not stated; the author used Node v10.10.0 in issue #1 a week earlier) hashed 1,000,000 random 1-1000 byte messages once each: the AssemblyScript Wasm build took 369.1 ms against 447.7 ms for the module's own JS port (about 1.21x, derived from page data), including the per-message copy into Wasm memory. Other published runs of the same benchmark range from Wasm 1.1x slower (pre-optimisation build) to 1.51x faster, so the gain is real but small and run-dependent.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-04-06 (9 commits, 19 stars, never published to npm), but ISC-licensed and only about 60 lines per implementation, so it is easy to vendor; fix the tail bytes to signed char first if you need reference-compatible hashes.
